The Traffic Rules

Chapter 1 contains the heart of Dutch traffic law — the rules that govern what every road user must and must not do at every moment. These rules apply to everyone: cyclists, moped riders, car drivers, truck drivers, pedestrians forming a procession, horse riders. No one on the road is exempt.

The rules are organised by topic. Each section covers one aspect of road behaviour. Together they form a complete picture of how Dutch roads are expected to function.

§ 1 — Position on the Road

Where each type of road user must travel — and on which part of the road.

Keep to the Right All drivers

Every driver is required to keep as far to the right as possible. This is the fundamental position rule — it applies on every road, in every situation, unless another rule specifically provides otherwise.

Cyclists may ride two abreast. Snorfiets riders may not — they must ride in single file.
▧Illustration plannedkeep-right-rule.webp
Where Pedestrians Must Walk Pedestrians

Pedestrians follow a strict order of preference for where they walk. First choice: pavement (trottoir) or footpath. If neither exists: the bicycle path or combined bicycle/moped path. If none of those exist either: the verge or the very edge of the carriageway.

People moving with non-vehicle objects — roller skates, a skateboard, a walking frame — use the bicycle path, footpath or pavement. If none of those are present, they use the carriageway.

▧Illustration plannedpedestrian-path-order.webp
Where Cyclists Must Ride Cyclists

Cyclists must use the mandatory bicycle path or combined bicycle/moped path where one is present. If no mandatory path exists, they use the carriageway. They may also use an optional (non-mandatory) bicycle path.

A snorfiets with a combustion engine may only use an optional bicycle path with its engine switched off.

Bicycles or bicycles-with-trailer that are wider than 0.75 metres (including load) may use the carriageway regardless.

On roads where a local traffic decision requires it — and where a sign below the mandatory bicycle path sign confirms this — snorfiets riders must use the carriageway instead of the bicycle path.
▧Illustration plannedcyclist-path-rules.webp
Where Moped Riders Must Ride Bromfiets

Moped riders (bromfietsers) use the combined bicycle/moped path. If none exists, they use the carriageway. Mopeds or mopeds-with-trailer wider than 0.75 metres (including load) always use the carriageway.

▧Illustration plannedmoped-path-rules.webp
Disability Vehicles Gehandicaptenvoertuig

Drivers of disability vehicles may use any of the following: the pavement, the footpath, the bicycle path, the combined bicycle/moped path, or the carriageway. They have full flexibility in choosing the most appropriate surface.

▧Illustration planneddisability-vehicle-paths.webp
Horse Riders Ruiters

Horse riders use the bridlepath (ruiterpad). If no bridlepath is present, they use the verge or the carriageway.

▧Illustration plannedhorse-rider-path.webp
All Other Drivers — and the Carriageway Rule Motor vehicles etc.

All drivers not covered by the specific rules above — car drivers, truck drivers, bus drivers — use the carriageway. For parking, they may also use other parts of the road except the pavement, footpath, bicycle path, combined bicycle/moped path or bridlepath.

Bicycle lanes with a solid continuous line may not be used by any driver other than cyclists and disability vehicle drivers.

▧Illustration plannedsolid-bike-lane-no-entry.webp
Pedestrian Columns on the Carriageway

Pedestrians who form a column, procession or funeral cortège may use the carriageway. When they do, the vehicle rules of the road apply to them — including traffic lights and road markings.

§ 2 — Overtaking

The default direction of overtaking — and the exceptions.

Overtake on the Left Default rule

The standard rule: overtaking happens on the left. You move to the left, pass the slower vehicle, and return to the right.

There are specific exceptions:

  • A driver who has moved to the left and signalled their intention to turn left is overtaken on the right.
  • Cyclists must overtake other cyclists on the left — but may overtake other types of drivers on the right.
  • A driver to the right of a block marking may overtake a driver to the left of that marking on the right.
  • Trams may be overtaken on the right.
▧Illustration plannedovertake-on-left.webp
No Overtaking at Pedestrian Crossings Prohibited

It is prohibited to overtake a vehicle immediately before or on a pedestrian crossing. The moment you approach a zebra crossing, overtaking must stop — regardless of how slow the vehicle ahead is moving.

▧Illustration plannedno-overtake-pedestrian-crossing.webp

§ 3 — Traffic Jams

Special rules that apply when traffic comes to a standstill.

Traffic Jam Rules File

When traffic is at a standstill or moving very slowly and the carriageway is divided into lanes in the same direction, you are not required to use the rightmost lane. Stay in whichever lane you are in.

When traffic is moving in queues, drivers may pass a queue on the right. This is an exception to the normal rule that overtaking takes place on the left.

▧Illustration plannedtraffic-jam-rules.webp
The Zip Merge (Ritsvoegsel)

When a lane ends and traffic must merge, Dutch road culture expects drivers to use the full length of the ending lane before merging — one car at a time, alternating. This is not legally mandated in the RVV but is consistently applied in practice and reinforced by road markings.

§ 4 — Entering Intersections

The single most important rule about intersections.

Do Not Block an Intersection Prohibited

Drivers may not block an intersection. This means: do not enter an intersection unless you can completely clear it. If traffic ahead is slow or stationary and you cannot pass through, wait before the intersection until the way is clear.

Blocking an intersection prevents cross-traffic from moving and is one of the most common causes of gridlock in cities.

▧Illustration planneddo-not-block-intersection.webp

§ 5 — Right of Way

Who goes first — the fundamental priority rules at intersections and level crossings.

Give Way to the Right Core rule

At intersections, all drivers must give way to drivers approaching from the right. This is the default rule when no signs, traffic lights or other rules indicate otherwise.

Two exceptions apply:

  • Drivers on an unpaved road must give way to drivers on a paved road — regardless of which side they come from.
  • At an otherwise unregulated intersection, drivers must give way to trams. Traffic lights, authorised traffic-controller instructions and applicable traffic signs can determine a different order.
▧Illustration plannedgive-way-to-right.webp
The Right-of-Way Hierarchy at Intersections

When you approach an unmarked intersection, ask yourself in this order: (1) Is there a traffic controller? Follow their instructions. (2) Are there traffic lights? Follow them. (3) Are there road signs (priority road, give way, stop)? Follow them. (4) None of the above? Apply the ordinary priority rules: give way to drivers from the right, with the statutory exceptions including trams and paved-versus-unpaved roads.

Behaviour at Level Crossings Overweg

A road user may only proceed onto a level crossing if they can pass through immediately and clear the crossing completely. You must never enter a level crossing unless you are certain you can get all the way across without stopping.

At a level crossing, all road users must let any rail vehicle pass — train, tram, metro — and must keep the crossing completely free while doing so.

▧Illustration plannedlevel-crossing-rules.webp

§ 6 — Military Convoys & Funeral Cortèges

Do Not Cut Through Prohibited

Road users are prohibited from cutting through a military convoy or a motor vehicle funeral cortège. If such a procession is crossing your path, you must wait until it has passed completely — even if you have right of way.

▧Illustration planneddo-not-cut-convoy.webp

§ 7 — Turning

How to signal, position and yield when making a turn.

Positioning Before a Turn Pre-turn

Before turning, a driver may move into the correct position:

  • Turning right: Move as far to the right as possible, in good time before the turn.
  • Turning left: Move as close to the centre line as possible — or, on a one-way road, as far to the left as possible.

Before turning, the driver must signal with their indicator or, if no indicator is fitted, with their arm.

▧Illustration plannedturn-positioning.webp
Giving Way When Turning Priority

A driver who is turning must give way to:

  • Traffic coming from the opposite direction on the same road.
  • Traffic travelling alongside them on the same road — to the left or right, or close behind.

A driver turning left must also give way to an oncoming driver who is turning right at the same intersection.

The ordinary turning-yield rules contain an exception for trams. Always also obey traffic lights, signs and authorised traffic-controller instructions.
▧Illustration plannedgive-way-when-turning.webp

§ 8 — Speed Limits

The general principle, the standard limits, and the special limits for specific vehicle types.

The Stopping Distance Principle Always applies

Before any specific speed limit applies, there is an overriding principle: a driver must always be able to stop within the distance they can see ahead of them — and within the distance that is clear. This means that even if you are within the speed limit, you are driving too fast if you cannot stop in time for what you can see.

The limits above must always be read together with the posted signs and electronic matrix signs. On Dutch motorways, the permitted speed depends on the road section and time of day. From 06:00 to 19:00, almost all motorways are limited to 100 km/h, with some sections at 80 or 130 km/h. From 19:00 to 06:00, many sections allow 100, 120 or 130 km/h. Always follow the limit shown for the road and time you are driving.

§ 9 — Stopping (Stilstaan)

Locations where stopping — even briefly — is prohibited.

Where You May Not Stop Prohibited locations

A driver may not stop their vehicle at any of the following locations:

  • At an intersection or a level crossing
  • On a bicycle lane, or on the carriageway alongside a bicycle lane
  • On a pedestrian crossing, or within 5 metres of one
  • Inside a tunnel
  • At a bus stop sign — at the level of the block marking, or within 12 metres of the sign if no marking is present
  • On the carriageway alongside a bus lane
  • Alongside a solid yellow line
The bus stop rule does not apply to immediately boarding or alighting passengers. You may briefly stop to let someone in or out at a bus stop, but you may not park there.
▧Illustration plannedno-stopping-locations.webp
▧Illustration plannedno-stop-intersection.webp
▧Illustration plannedno-stop-bike-lane.webp
▧Illustration plannedno-stop-pedestrian-crossing.webp
▧Illustration plannedno-stop-tunnel.webp
▧Illustration plannedno-stop-bus-stop.webp
▧Illustration plannedno-stop-yellow-line.webp

§ 10 — Parking

Where you may not leave your vehicle — and the rules for marked parking spaces.

Where You May Not Park Prohibited locations

Parking is prohibited at the following locations:

  • Within 5 metres of an intersection
  • In front of an entrance or exit (driveway)
  • On a priority road carriageway outside a built-up area
  • In a parking space, if your vehicle does not belong to the category shown on the sign
  • In a parking space, in a manner or for a purpose different from what is shown on the sign
  • At a location or time when parking is prohibited by a sign
  • Along a broken yellow line (parking prohibited)
  • On a pedestrian crossing or within 5 metres of one (same as stopping)
  • On a cycle path or footpath
  • Alongside another parked vehicle (double parking)
▧Illustration plannedparking-prohibited-locations.webp
Time-Limited Parking Parkeerschijf

Where a sign indicates time-limited parking with a blue zone (blauwe zone), the driver must display a parking disc (parkeerschijf) showing the time of arrival. The disc must be clearly visible through the windscreen. Parking beyond the permitted time shown on the sign is prohibited.

▧Illustration plannedparking-disc-blue-zone.webp
Paid Parking Betaald parkeren

Where paid parking applies, the driver must comply with the payment method and conditions indicated for that location. Payment may be made by a parking machine, parking app or another authorised method. A paper ticket only needs to be displayed when the local system requires it. Parking without valid payment, or beyond the paid period, is prohibited.

▧Illustration plannedpaid-parking-sign.webp
Stopping vs Parking — A Quick Reminder

Everything in §9 (stopping) is also prohibited for parking. But parking has many additional prohibited locations on top of those. A location that allows brief stopping may still prohibit parking. Always check for signs.

§ 11 — Placing Bicycles & Mopeds

Parking Bikes and Mopeds Cyclists & riders

Bicycles and mopeds must be placed in a way that does not obstruct other road users. They may not be placed on a carriageway, cycle path, pavement or footpath in a manner that prevents pedestrians, cyclists or other users from passing freely. Where dedicated bicycle parking areas exist, they must be used.

▧Illustration plannedbicycle-parking-rules.webp

§ 12 — Signals & Identification Markings

How to signal your intentions — and the legally prescribed signals and identification markings used in special situations.

Signalling Your Intentions All drivers

Drivers must give clear, timely signals when they intend to change direction or position. Signals are given using the indicator (richtingaanwijzer). If no indicator is fitted, an arm signal must be used instead. Signals must be given before the manoeuvre begins — not during it.

▧Illustration plannedindicator-arm-signal.webp
Priority Vehicle Signals 🚨 Emergency

A priority vehicle uses both a flashing blue light and a siren simultaneously. These signals may only be used when the vehicle is responding to an emergency. All other road users must give way immediately and completely to a vehicle displaying both signals.

The blue flashing light and siren may also be used without the vehicle qualifying as a priority vehicle — for example, a police vehicle stopping someone. In that case, the full priority vehicle rules do not automatically apply, but road users must still respond appropriately.

▧Illustration plannedpriority-vehicle-lights-siren.webp
Military Convoy Markings

Military convoys display officially designated identification markings agreed upon by the Minister of Infrastructure and the Minister of Defence. These markings distinguish a military convoy from regular traffic and alert other road users that the convoy may not be cut through.

▧Illustration plannedmilitary-convoy-markings.webp
Funeral Cortège Markings

A recognised motor-vehicle funeral cortège uses the legally prescribed identification signs. These consist of two black triangular flags fitted to the participating vehicles in the prescribed manner. Do not confuse these markings with orange or purple rotating lights.

▧Illustration plannedfuneral-cortege-markings.webp
Horn and Light Signals Warning signals

Drivers may use sound signals or flashing-light signals only to avert imminent danger. The rule applies both inside and outside built-up areas. The horn or headlight flash must therefore not be used merely as a greeting, to express frustration, or simply to announce an intention to overtake.

Using the horn unnecessarily or as a noise nuisance is covered separately in §25 (unnecessary noise).
▧Illustration plannedhorn-flash-warning.webp

§ 13 — Lights While Moving

Which lights must be on, and when, while the vehicle is in motion.

Motor Vehicles — Front Lights Motorvoertuigen

Motor vehicles must use dipped headlights (dimlichten) during the night and in conditions of reduced visibility — fog, rain, snow, or dusk. During the day in good visibility, daytime running lights (dagrijverlichting) are sufficient if the vehicle is equipped with them. Headlights must not blind other road users.

▧Illustration planneddipped-headlights.webp
Bicycles — Lighting Requirements Cyclists

A bicycle being ridden at night or in poor visibility must have:

  • A white or yellow front light that does not flash
  • A red rear light that does not flash
  • A red rear reflector (not triangular)
  • Amber/yellow pedal reflectors
  • White or yellow reflectors on the wheels/rims or tyres
▧Illustration plannedbicycle-lights-night.webp
Rear Lights & Reflectors All vehicles

All vehicles must display red rear lights during the night and in poor visibility. In addition, they must carry the required reflectors — positions and colours vary by vehicle type but the principle is universal: your vehicle must be visible from behind.

▧Illustration plannedrear-lights-reflectors.webp
Fog Lights Poor visibility

Front fog lights may be used when fog, snowfall or rain seriously reduces visibility. Rear fog lights may only be used when fog or snowfall reduces visibility to less than 50 metres; they may not be used merely because of heavy rain. Switch fog lights off when the conditions no longer justify their use.

▧Illustration plannedfog-lights-use.webp
Orange Rotating Light Slow vehicles

An amber/yellow rotating or flashing light is used in legally specified situations to warn other road users of a special or dangerous situation, for example certain road works, recovery operations or exceptional transports. It does not give the vehicle priority.

▧Illustration plannedorange-rotating-light.webp

§ 14 — Lights While Stationary

Lighting obligations when your vehicle is stopped or parked.

Lighting When Parked at Night Night parking

At night — and during the day when visibility is seriously reduced — a motor vehicle that is stationary outside a built-up area on the carriageway must show the prescribed front and rear parking/position lights. The same lighting obligation applies on parking strips, parking bays, emergency lanes and emergency bays along motorways and expressways.

Inside built-up areas, the specific stationary-lighting obligation above does not apply in the same way; always make sure the vehicle is safely and lawfully positioned and sufficiently visible.

▧Illustration plannedparking-lights-night.webp

§ 15 — Special Lights

Blue Flashing Light Emergency services

A blue flashing or rotating light may only be used by vehicles for which this is officially authorised — principally ambulances, fire trucks and police vehicles. It signals an emergency and, combined with a siren, creates a priority vehicle.

▧Illustration plannedblue-flashing-light.webp
Green Flashing Light Specific use

A green flashing light is reserved for the command vehicle associated with authorised police, fire-brigade or ambulance operations. It identifies a command function; it does not by itself make the vehicle a priority vehicle or create a right of way.

▧Illustration plannedgreen-flashing-light.webp

§ 16 — Motorways & Expressways

Special rules that apply only on autosnelwegen (motorways) and autowegen (expressways).

Who May Not Use a Motorway Restricted access

The following road users are prohibited from using a motorway:

  • Pedestrians
  • Cyclists
  • Moped riders (both bromfiets and snorfiets)
  • Disability vehicle drivers
  • Horse riders and animal handlers
  • Vehicles that, by construction, cannot or may not travel at least 60 km/h
  • Agricultural vehicles and slow motor vehicles
▧Illustration plannedmotorway-restricted-users.webp
Motorway Behaviour Rules Autosnelweg

On a motorway, the following are prohibited:

  • Stopping, turning around or reversing
  • Crossing the central reservation
  • Driving on the emergency shoulder — except in an emergency, or when it is officially opened as a rush-hour lane
  • Driving on or over a diversion area (verdrijvingsvlak)

Entry and exit may only happen via the designated entry lanes (invoegstroken) and exit lanes (uitrijstroken).

▧Illustration plannedmotorway-rules.webp
Expressway (Autoweg) Rules G3 sign

An autoweg (sign G3) is intended for motor vehicles that, by construction, can and may travel at least 50 km/h. It is not the same as a motorway and may have at-grade intersections or different access arrangements. Always follow the signs and markings that apply to the particular road.

▧Illustration plannedexpressway-sign-g3.webp
Rush-Hour Lane (Spitsstrook)

During peak hours, the emergency shoulder on certain motorways is opened as an additional driving lane — the spitsstrook. Electronic signs above the road confirm whether it is open. When it is open, you may use it as a normal lane. When the signs show a red cross, the lane is closed and you must not drive on it.

§ 17 — Residential Zones (Erven)

Special rules for areas where pedestrians and vehicles share the same space.

Speed in an Erf 15 km/h maximum

Inside an erf, drivers may not travel faster than 15 km/h. This is the statutory maximum speed. Because pedestrians may use the full width of the road, drivers must remain especially alert and be able to respond safely.

▧Illustration plannederf-walking-pace.webp
Pedestrians May Use the Full Width Shared space

Inside an erf, pedestrians may use the full width of the road. This does not create a blanket rule that pedestrians automatically have right of way over every driver; the normal priority and manoeuvre rules still matter. Drivers must nevertheless adapt their behaviour to the shared-space character of the erf and avoid creating danger.

▧Illustration plannederf-pedestrian-priority.webp
Parking in an Erf Marked spots only

Parking inside an erf is only permitted in designated marked parking spaces. You may not park on any other part of the erf — not on the road surface, not on the shared walking area.

▧Illustration plannederf-parking-marked-only.webp
Leaving an Erf Exiting

When leaving a residential zone (erf) onto a normal road, drivers must give way to all traffic on that road — both from the left and from the right.

▧Illustration plannederf-exit-give-way.webp
Erf Sign

The erf zone begins at a white sign showing a house and a pedestrian figure. The zone ends at the same sign with a diagonal red line through it. Inside the zone, all the special rules above apply.

§ 18 — Roundabouts

Priority on a Roundabout Give way to traffic on the roundabout

Priority at a roundabout is determined by the signs and road markings. On most Dutch roundabouts, give-way signs and shark's teeth require entering drivers to give way to traffic already on the roundabout. If no priority signs or markings regulate the roundabout, the ordinary rule of giving way to drivers approaching from the right applies; in that situation, traffic entering from the right can have priority.

Do not assume that traffic already on every roundabout automatically has priority. Read the signs and shark's teeth at the specific roundabout.
▧Illustration plannedroundabout-priority.webp
Signalling on a Roundabout Indicators

When leaving a roundabout, signal right before your exit. You do not need to signal when entering or when passing exits you are not taking. The key moment to signal is just before you exit, so drivers waiting to enter know you are leaving.

▧Illustration plannedroundabout-signalling.webp

§ 19 — Pedestrians

Give Way to Pedestrians at Crossings Pedestrian crossings

Drivers must give way to pedestrians who are on a pedestrian crossing or who are clearly about to step onto one. This applies to all zebra crossings. A pedestrian who has stepped onto the crossing, or who is standing at the edge clearly waiting to cross, has priority.

Cyclists also have priority at crossings marked with both zebra stripes and bicycle symbols (combined crossing).

▧Illustration plannedpedestrian-crossing-priority.webp

§ 20 — Priority Vehicles

Make Way Immediately 🚨 Emergency

When a priority vehicle — one displaying both a blue flashing light and a siren — approaches, all other road users must give way immediately. This means:

  • Move to the side as quickly as safely possible
  • Stop if necessary
  • Do not block the path of the priority vehicle
  • This applies even if it means briefly stopping on a yellow line or in another location where stopping is normally prohibited
Making way for a priority vehicle does not mean you can ignore traffic lights or endanger other road users. Act as safely as possible.
▧Illustration plannedpriority-vehicle-make-way.webp

§ 21 — Loose Animals on the Road

Animals on the Road Caution required

When encountering loose animals on or near the road — livestock, horses, dogs — all road users must slow down and take precautions. Animals are unpredictable; sudden movements are common. Pass slowly and give as much space as possible. Do not use the horn near animals as this can startle them further.

▧Illustration plannedanimals-on-road.webp

§ 22 — Boarding & Alighting Passengers

Give Way When Boarding or Alighting Trams & buses

When a tram or bus is stopped and passengers are boarding or alighting, other road users must give way to those passengers. Passengers stepping off a tram or bus and crossing the road have priority — even if they are not at a formal pedestrian crossing.

▧Illustration plannedtram-bus-passengers-boarding.webp

§ 23 — Towing a Vehicle

Towing Rules Slepen

When one motor vehicle tows another, the distance from the rear of the towing vehicle to the front of the towed vehicle may be no more than 5 metres. The towing arrangement must be safe and the towed vehicle must remain controllable.

The RVV provision on towing does not set a general 25 km/h towing limit. Do not memorise 25 km/h as a universal Dutch towing rule. On motorways and expressways, the separate access and safety rules must also be respected; an unsafe or unsuitable towing situation should be handled by professional recovery services.

▧Illustration plannedtowing-broken-vehicle.webp

§ 24 — Special Manoeuvres

Reversing, turning around, and other manoeuvres that require extra care.

Give Way Before Any Special Manoeuvre Always yield first

Before performing any special manoeuvre — reversing, turning around (U-turn), moving from a parking space, pulling away from the kerb, changing lanes — the driver must first give way to all other traffic. No special manoeuvre may be started if it would force another road user to change speed or direction.

▧Illustration plannedspecial-manoeuvre-yield.webp
Reversing Achteruit rijden

Reversing is only permitted when it can be done safely and without hindering other road users. You must check behind you — use mirrors and look over your shoulder. Reversing at speed or over a long distance on a public road is generally not permitted.

▧Illustration plannedreversing-safely.webp
U-Turn Keren

A U-turn (keermanoeuvre) is only permitted when it can be completed safely, without obstructing other road users, and without endangering anyone. It is prohibited on motorways and expressways. It may also be prohibited by specific road signs.

▧Illustration plannedu-turn-rules.webp

§ 25 — Unnecessary Noise

No Unnecessary Noise Prohibited

It is prohibited to make unnecessary noise with a vehicle. This includes unnecessary revving of the engine, repeated horn use for non-safety reasons, and unnecessarily loud exhaust systems. The horn exists solely as a safety warning device — not as a communication tool or expression of frustration.

▧Illustration plannedno-unnecessary-noise.webp

§ 26 — Warning Triangle

When to Place a Warning Triangle Gevarendriehoek

A warning triangle is not mandatory equipment to carry in a car in the Netherlands. If a stationary motor vehicle with more than two wheels, or a trailer, forms an obstacle that approaching drivers may not notice in time, those drivers must be warned. This can be done with the vehicle's hazard warning lights or with a warning triangle. If the hazard warning lights are operating, a triangle is not required. When a triangle is used, place it about 30 metres from the vehicle in the direction from which traffic approaches.

▧Illustration plannedwarning-triangle-placement.webp

§ 26a — Seating

Only Use Designated Seats Zitplaatsen

Passengers may only occupy designated seats in or on a vehicle. Standing in a moving vehicle, sitting in the boot, or occupying a position not designed for passengers is prohibited unless the vehicle is specifically designed for that purpose (e.g. certain buses).

▧Illustration planneddesignated-seats-only.webp

§ 27 — Seatbelts & Child Restraints

Seatbelt Mandatory Autogordel

All occupants of a motor vehicle must wear a seatbelt while the vehicle is moving. The driver is responsible for ensuring that passengers under 18 are properly restrained. The seatbelt must be worn correctly — across the shoulder and chest, not tucked under the arm.

▧Illustration plannedseatbelt-mandatory.webp
Child Safety Systems Children under 1.35m

Children under 1.35 metres tall must generally use an approved child restraint system suitable for the child and fitted correctly. Children may be carried in an approved child seat in the front or rear. A rear-facing child seat may only be used on a seat with a front airbag if that airbag has been deactivated.

▧Illustration plannedchild-seat-requirement.webp
Seatbelt Exemptions

Certain occupants are exempt from the seatbelt requirement — for example, people with a medical certificate confirming they cannot wear a seatbelt, drivers reversing, and some professional categories. Exemptions are listed on a special card which must be carried in the vehicle.

§ 28 — Helmets

Helmet Obligation Bromfiets & Motorfiets

The driver and any passenger of a motorcycle or moped (bromfiets) must wear an approved helmet that is properly fastened while the vehicle is moving. The helmet must meet the required safety standard.

Snorfiets riders and their passengers must also wear an approved helmet. A snorfiets rider may use an approved moped helmet or an approved speed-pedelec helmet. Speed-pedelec riders and passengers are likewise subject to an approved-helmet requirement.

Vehicle-specific exemptions can exist where the law expressly provides for them, for example for certain vehicles equipped with an approved safety cell. Do not treat a safety cell as a general personal exemption from the helmet rules.

▧Illustration plannedhelmet-obligation.webp

§ 29 — Children on Bicycles & Mopeds

Carrying Children Age & seat rules

Children under 8 years old carried on a bicycle, snorfiets or bromfiets must have a safe seating position that provides sufficient support for the back, hands and feet — for example, a suitable child seat. Children carried on a bromfiets or snorfiets must also comply with the applicable helmet requirement.

The rules focus on a safe, properly supported seating position; there is no general Dutch traffic rule that only one child may ever be carried on a bicycle. The number of passengers must be compatible with the vehicle's design and safe use.

▧Illustration plannedchild-seat-on-bicycle.webp

§ 30 — Mobile Phones While Driving

No Handheld Phone Use Prohibited

It is prohibited to hold and use a mobile phone — or any other handheld electronic communication device — while driving. This applies to all drivers: car drivers, cyclists, moped riders, and all others.

The prohibition concerns holding a mobile electronic device while driving. Hands-free use is permitted in principle for drivers, including cyclists and moped riders, provided the device is not held and its use does not create danger or hinder traffic. A securely mounted device may therefore be used without holding it, but safe attention to traffic remains essential.

The prohibition applies to all forms of handheld use: calling, texting, navigating, checking apps. If you need to use your phone, stop safely first.
▧Illustration plannedno-phone-while-driving.webp
This Applies to Cyclists Too

The mobile phone prohibition is frequently assumed to apply only to car drivers. It applies to all drivers, including cyclists. Riding a bicycle while holding a phone is prohibited and carries a fine.

§ 31 — Carrying Passengers in Trailers & Load Spaces

General Prohibition Passengers in trailers

It is generally prohibited to carry passengers in trailers, in the load space of a vehicle, or in the open load area of a truck. Passengers must always travel in the enclosed passenger compartment of a vehicle — not in or on a trailer being towed.

Specific exceptions exist for certain agricultural vehicles, vehicles used for organised trips with special authorisation, and historic vehicles under supervision. These exceptions require specific permits or conditions to be met.

▧Illustration plannedno-passengers-in-trailer.webp
Chapter 1 — What to Take Away

Chapter 1 covers core active rules of the road: where to drive, how to signal, when to yield, how speed limits work, when stopping or parking is prohibited, and which safety requirements apply. Key principles include keeping right, giving way to drivers from the right at equivalent unregulated intersections, respecting tram priority where the ordinary rules require it, not blocking intersections, signalling important lateral movements, seatbelt and helmet requirements, and the ban on holding a mobile electronic device while driving.

For speed questions, distinguish the statutory default from the limit actually shown on the road. In particular, motorway limits depend on the road section, signs and time of day. For stopping and parking, remember the difference between a solid yellow line (no stopping) and a broken yellow line (no parking).
